Description: Five years after the Great Fire of 1845 burned a third of Pittsburgh, the rebuilt brick city of 46,000 smokes with glassworks, rolling mills, foundries and boatyards. Choose your industry and where to found your works.
Irish refugees from the Great Famine and Germans fleeing the failed revolutions of 1848 arrive by canal and river, settling in the Point, Lawrenceville and Allegheny City.
The first railroad reaches Allegheny City from the west, beginning the end of the canal era.
The Pennsylvania Railroad opens its line over the mountains. Philadelphia is now hours, not days, away; the canal and the Conestoga wagon fade.
Cholera sweeps the crowded riverfront wards. Hundreds die; families flee to the hills.
A financial panic spreads from New York. Iron prices collapse and mills bank their furnaces.
Edwin Drake strikes oil up the Allegheny. Refineries spring up along Pittsburgh's riverbanks and barges of crude crowd the wharves.
President-elect Lincoln speaks at the Monongahela House on his way to Washington.
The Union calls for men and guns. The Fort Pitt Foundry casts great Rodman cannon; every mill runs night and day.
An explosion tears through the Allegheny Arsenal's cartridge laboratory in Lawrenceville, killing 78 workers, most of them young women.

Event Name: Defences Thrown Up on the Hills
Description: As Lee's army invades Pennsylvania, thousands of workers dig earthworks on the hills around the city. The rebels turn back at Gettysburg.
Peace returns. War contracts end, but railroads and cities across the country need iron as never before.
Allegheny City turns its old common pasture into a landscaped public park.
A visiting writer describes the smoky valley at night as 'hell with the lid off'. The name sticks.

Event Name: The City Annexes the East End
Description: Pittsburgh annexes Lawrenceville, Oakland, East Liberty and the farms beyond, tripling its area.
The first passenger incline lifts workers up Coal Hill to the new streets of Mt. Washington.

Event Name: The South Side Joins the City
Description: Birmingham and the other South Side boroughs are annexed to Pittsburgh.
The collapse of Jay Cooke's bank starts the Long Depression. Orders vanish; wages are cut across the valley.
Andrew Carnegie's Edgar Thomson Works at Braddock rolls its first Bessemer steel rail. A new age of steel begins.
Railroad workers strike against wage cuts. Militia fire on a crowd at 28th Street; the crowd burns the Pennsylvania Railroad's roundhouse and hundreds of cars.
Slovak, Hungarian, Polish and Rusyn labourers begin arriving for mill jobs, recruited by agents and letters home.
The Pittsburgh Bessemer Steel Company opens a works on the Homestead flats. Carnegie buys it two years later.
Father Mollinger completes St. Anthony's Chapel on Troy Hill, with thousands of relics. Pilgrims arrive by the trainload.
Gustav Lindenthal's lenticular truss bridge replaces Roebling's suspension span over the Monongahela.
Natural gas is piped into Pittsburgh's mills and homes. For a few years the smoke thins and the sky turns blue.
George Westinghouse founds his electric company to sell alternating current. The battle of the currents begins.
H. H. Richardson's massive stone courthouse and jail open on Grant's Hill.
The South Fork Dam, owned by a club of Pittsburgh industrialists, fails upriver. More than 2,200 die in Johnstown; relief trains leave from Pittsburgh.

Event Name: Schenley Park Given to the City
Description: Mary Schenley gives 300 acres of land in Oakland for a great public park.
The Carnegie Free Library of Allegheny opens, the first of the libraries Andrew Carnegie will give to American towns.
Locked-out steelworkers fight Pinkerton guards landing from barges at the Homestead Works. Seven workers and three Pinkertons die; the state militia occupies the town and the union is broken.
Anarchist Alexander Berkman shoots and stabs Henry Clay Frick in his office downtown. Frick survives and returns to work within a week.
Banks and railroads fail across the country. Mills close; soup kitchens open in the mill towns.
Carnegie's library, music hall and museum open in Oakland.
Carnegie's Union Railroad links his works along the Monongahela, moving hot metal and ore between mills.
J. P. Morgan buys Carnegie Steel for $480 million and forms the United States Steel Corporation, the first billion-dollar company. Dozens of Pittsburgh men become millionaires overnight.
The Pittsburgh Pirates play Boston in the first modern World Series. Boston wins.
The rivers rise to 36 feet. Downtown streets and the riverfront mills are under water for days.
A run on the banks spreads from New York. Orders are cancelled and furnaces banked.
After a long legal fight, the city of Allegheny is annexed to Pittsburgh and becomes the North Side.
Social investigators document twelve-hour shifts, seven-day weeks, industrial deaths and typhoid in the mill districts.
The city's sand filtration plant opens. Typhoid deaths, once the worst in the nation, fall sharply.
Immigrant workers at McKees Rocks strike against the 'pool' pay system. State troopers and strikebreakers clash with strikers; a dozen die.
The Pirates open their steel-and-concrete ballpark in Oakland.
Honus Wagner and the Pirates beat Ty Cobb's Detroit Tigers.
Downtown's Grant's Hill is lowered by fourteen feet to level the streets around the courthouse.
War breaks out in Europe. Immigration stops almost overnight while orders for steel and shells pour in.
Black families from the South arrive for mill jobs left open by the war, settling in the Hill District, Homestead and Beltzhoover.
The United States declares war on Germany. The mills run at full capacity; German street names are changed.
The influenza pandemic hits Pittsburgh harder than almost any American city. Schools, churches and saloons close.
The war ends on November 11. Steel orders fall away.
Some 350,000 steelworkers walk out nationwide demanding union recognition and the eight-hour day. Strikers are arrested and meetings banned; the strike collapses by January.
The saloons close. Speakeasies open in back rooms in every neighbourhood.
Westinghouse's KDKA in East Pittsburgh makes the first commercial radio broadcast, reporting the Harding-Cox election returns.
Congress passes emergency immigration quotas. The great waves from Southern and Eastern Europe come to an end.
Under public pressure, U.S. Steel ends the twelve-hour shift.
Permanent quotas all but close immigration from Southern and Eastern Europe. The mill towns' ethnic neighbourhoods stop growing from abroad.
The University of Pittsburgh starts building its 42-storey Gothic skyscraper in Oakland.
Three matching self-anchored suspension bridges open over the Allegheny at Sixth, Seventh and Ninth Streets.
The stock market collapses. By 1932 the mills run at a fifth of capacity.
Father James Cox of Old St. Patrick's leads 25,000 unemployed Pittsburghers to Washington to demand relief.
Prohibition ends. The saloons and clubs reopen legally.
The worst flood in the city's history crests at 46 feet. Downtown is under water to the second floor, the mills stand idle and power fails for days.
Philip Murray's SWOC opens offices in the mill towns and signs up workers in secret.
U.S. Steel recognises the union without a strike. Two months later Jones & Laughlin's men strike and win too.
War breaks out in Europe. Orders for steel climb.
America enters the war. The valley becomes the arsenal of democracy; Dravo builds landing ships on Neville Island.
SWOC becomes the United Steelworkers of America.
Business and civic leaders under Richard King Mellon form a council to clean up the smoke and rebuild downtown.
The war ends. Workers and veterans want higher wages and better homes.
Three-quarters of a million steelworkers strike nationwide for higher wages.
The city's smoke ordinance takes effect for homes and mills. Coal gives way to natural gas and the skies begin to clear.
A temperature inversion traps smoke from the zinc works in Donora, up the Monongahela. Twenty die; thousands fall ill.
The old warehouse district at the Point is cleared for Gateway Center and Point State Park.
President Truman seizes the steel industry to prevent a wartime strike. The Supreme Court overturns the seizure and the men walk out.
Bulldozers clear the Lower Hill District for a civic arena, displacing 8,000 residents and hundreds of businesses.
The first full-scale nuclear power plant in America begins sending power to Pittsburgh.
The longest steel strike in history. Customers turn to imported steel and many never come back.
Bill Mazeroski's ninth-inning home run wins the World Series for the Pirates over the Yankees.
The domed arena with its retractable stainless-steel roof opens in the cleared Lower Hill.
After the murder of Martin Luther King, Jr., unrest breaks out in the Hill District and Homewood.
The Pirates and Steelers move to a new stadium on the North Side.
Roberto Clemente leads the Pirates to a World Series title.
Franco Harris's last-second catch gives the Steelers their first playoff win.
The Arab oil embargo sends energy prices soaring. Detroit's car sales, and its steel orders, fall.
The fountain at the Point is turned on, completing the park where Fort Pitt stood.
The Steelers win their first Super Bowl.
The Pirates win the World Series and the Steelers will win a fourth Super Bowl in January.
U.S. Steel announces the shutdown of plants across the country. Imports, old open hearths and lost markets catch up with the valley.
Steel demand collapses in a deep recession. Layoffs spread through every mill town.
Nearly one in five workers in the Monongahela Valley is out of work. Food banks open in union halls.
U.S. Steel shuts the Duquesne Works. A campaign to save its giant 'Dorothy Six' blast furnace fails.
Jones & Laughlin's Pittsburgh works and most of the Homestead Works have closed. The steel era is ending; what the valley does next is up to those who remain.
